travixo.prose1: TraviXO is compliance software built for the French equipment rental industry. The system gives teams one place to track equipment, manage compliance, and see what needs attention next.
travixo.prose2: Time inside the equipment rental industry at Loxam put me close to how these operations actually run. The deeper picture of how VGP compliance fails came from studying the regulation and from conversations with rental teams.
travixo.prose3: Over time, the same failure points kept surfacing. Inspections get missed. Certificates end up scattered across emails or folders. The audit trail depends on someone remembering to keep it updated. The system was built around removing those failure points.

The same board fits a syndic chasing a gestionnaire's validation, a technical team waiting on a supplier's part, or a négoce holding an order until a delivery is confirmed. The tools already exist. The point is what happens between them.

travixo.title: A compliance system for the equipment rental industry.
travixo.standfirst: A live multi-tenant SaaS that manages VGP regulatory inspections for French equipment rental companies. Built solo, grounded in real industry constraints.

whatItIs.title: Compliance for the French equipment rental industry.
whatItIs.p1: TraviXO Systems is a multi-tenant compliance SaaS for the French equipment rental industry. It tracks the periodic regulatory inspections, the VGP, that every rental company in France is legally required to perform on the equipment they put in front of customers.
whatItIs.p2: Missed inspections are a liability problem and a regulatory problem, and the way most rental companies track them today is through a mix of paper folders, individual spreadsheets, and the memory of whoever has been there longest.
whatItIs.p3: The understanding behind it comes from time spent inside the equipment rental industry, close to how this work actually gets done. The product is shaped around those workflows rather than around a generic compliance template.
whatItIs.p4: Built solo. Deployed to a production environment as a Deralis product, covering the real regulatory VGP process.

whatIBuilt.title: The pieces that make the system work.

1.title: Multi-tenant foundation
1.body: Each rental company operates in its own isolated workspace, with strict separation of data between tenants.

2.title: Equipment register
2.body: Every piece of rentable equipment is tracked with its identification, category, regulatory class, and inspection schedule. The register is the single source of truth that every other part of the system depends on.

3.title: Inspection workflow
3.body: Inspections are scheduled automatically based on regulatory frequency, surfaced as work to do, and recorded with the inspector identity, date, findings, and any required follow-up. Nothing is recorded on paper and forgotten.

4.title: Audit trail and exports
4.body: Every action is logged in a way that survives an audit by the regulator. Inspection records can be exported as compliance reports without anyone having to assemble a folder by hand the night before.

5.title: Role-aware access
5.body: The branch manager, the technician, and the head office accountant see different views of the same data. Each role sees what is theirs to act on, and only that.

recognition.h2: If you’re here, it’s probably not by accident.
recognition.intro1: Your business runs. Clients are served, invoices go out, teams do the work.
recognition.intro2: It’s not a willpower problem, and it’s not a team problem.
symptoms: You already have tools in place, but information still moves poorly between them.
The CRM says one thing, the ERP another, and the team ends up checking elsewhere.
To answer a simple question, you need to cross-reference multiple sources before trusting the answer.
Edge cases live elsewhere: personal files, emails, individual memory.
When someone is away, nobody can say where their files stand.
recognition.closing1: At this point, the question is no longer whether there’s a problem. You already know.
recognition.closing2: The question is: what’s the right first move. New software? A process change? Nothing at all? Should you build, buy, or better use what’s already there?
recognition.closing3: That’s the question the diagnostic answers. Not in theory. On your operation, with your constraints, in five business days.
recognition.count1: One is enough to be worth looking at.
recognition.count2: Two usually means the cost is already recurring.
recognition.count3: Recognise three or more? The problem is probably not caused by one person. It comes from the way the work is organised.

friction.warning: Check that this is hours per person per week, not the team total.

hours.label: Contracted weekly hours
hours.help: The number of hours each person is contracted to work per week.
hours.help2: For day-rate contracts, enter an equivalent weekly basis.

form.invalid: Check your entries. Time absorbed cannot exceed contracted weekly hours.
form.privacy: The calculation runs entirely in your browser. None of your figures are sent, stored or shared with any third party.

result.caption: The value of paid working time absorbed by these frictions.
result.rateLine: That represents approximately {rate} of the working time of the team concerned.
result.disclaimer: This amount is not an accounting loss or a direct cash expense. It values the share of employer cost associated with the time entered. The amount that could actually be recovered depends on the processes, volumes, constraints, and how the released capacity would be used.

next.p1: It does not yet show which frictions can genuinely be removed or whether fixing them would justify the investment.
next.p2: During the diagnostic, I look at how the work really happens: how many requests or jobs move through the business, where they slow down and which problems can actually be fixed. You then know what to fix first, and why.

method.title: How the calculation works
method.intro: The result uses the following formula:
method.formula: People affected × average annual employer cost × share of weekly time absorbed
method.shareIntro: The share of time absorbed is calculated as:
method.shareFormula: Weekly friction hours ÷ contracted weekly hours
method.p1: This approach values the time consumed using capacity cost principles drawn from Kaplan and Anderson's Time-Driven Activity-Based Costing.
method.p2: ISEOR's research also documents the economic effects of dysfunctions in work organization, time management, communication, and coordination. This simplified calculator is not an ISEOR diagnosis.
method.p3: It divides by contracted hours rather than practical capacity, which runs at roughly 80 to 85 percent of theoretical. The estimate is therefore deliberately conservative.
method.sourceTdabc: Harvard Business School · Time-Driven Activity-Based Costing
method.legal: This is an indicative, non-contractual estimate based solely on the information entered. It is not a guaranteed saving or a promise of revenue or growth.
